items.prompt: Which layer of the atmosphere, right at ground level, holds nearly all the air we breathe?

options.label: The stratosphere
options.feedback: The stratosphere sits well above the ground, far too thin and dry to be the air we breathe.

options.label: The troposphere
options.feedback: Gravity holds most of the atmosphere's mass in this lowest layer, pressed close to the surface.

options.label: The mesosphere
options.feedback: The mesosphere lies far higher up, too thin to sustain breathing.

options.label: The thermosphere
options.feedback: The thermosphere is so high and so thin that a person could not breathe there at all.

items.ok_line: Nearly all the air you have ever breathed came from one thin shell.
items.ko_line: The layer that holds most of the air is the one closest to the ground, not one further out.
items.exp_title: Where nearly all the air sits
items.exp_text: Gravity pulls the atmosphere's gas close to the planet, so it is packed far more tightly near the surface than higher up. The layer that results from that packing is the lowest and thinnest of all the layers by height. Nearly all the air we breathe sits in the troposphere.

items.prompt: Why does the air get thinner the higher you climb through the atmosphere?

options.label: Because gravity holds most of the air's mass close to the surface
options.feedback: Gravity pulls hardest on the air nearest the ground, packing it tightly there and leaving less to spread out above.

options.label: Because the air higher up turns into a different gas
options.feedback: The gases making up air do not change into new substances as altitude increases; they simply become more spread out.

options.label: Because sunlight burns the air away at height
options.feedback: Sunlight warms the air but does not destroy it or make it vanish.

options.label: Because wind blows the air sideways away from high places
options.feedback: Wind moves air around, but it does not carry it permanently off to leave high places thinner.

items.ok_line: Most of the air stays where gravity keeps it: near the ground.
items.ko_line: Thinking gets you further than picking the disappearing act.
items.exp_text: Gravity pulls every molecule of air toward the ground, so the molecules nearest the surface are squeezed close together by the weight of all the air above them. Further up, there is less air left above to press down, so the molecules there sit far more loosely spread out. The air gets thinner with height because gravity holds most of the air's mass close to the surface.

items.prompt: Why does it usually get colder as you climb higher through the troposphere?

options.label: Because clouds block the sun more the higher you go
options.feedback: Clear mountain air at height often sees more direct sun, not less, yet it is still colder there.

options.label: Because wind speeds increase with height and that alone chills the air
options.feedback: Wind can make cold feel sharper, but the air itself is already colder at height before any wind is considered.

options.label: Because the sun mainly warms the ground, and air far from it receives less of that warmth
options.feedback: The ground absorbs sunlight and passes warmth to the air just above it, so air further from the ground stays cooler.

options.label: Because oxygen carries less heat than it does near sea level
options.feedback: The proportion of oxygen in the air stays about the same with height; that isn't what changes the temperature.

items.ok_line: Heat rises out of the ground first, and air only gets what's left as it goes up.
items.ko_line: Ask what actually warms the air in the first place, and where that warmth comes from.
items.exp_text: Sunlight passes through the lower atmosphere without warming it very much and heats the solid ground instead. The ground then passes that warmth upward into the air directly above it, so air near the surface stays warmest and air further from the ground receives less of it. It usually gets colder with height because the sun mainly warms the ground, and air far from it receives less of that warmth.

items.prompt: What lies directly above the troposphere, where the temperature starts rising again with height instead of falling?

options.label: The mesosphere
options.feedback: The mesosphere sits higher still, above the layer where temperature turns and starts rising.

options.label: The exosphere
options.feedback: The exosphere is the outermost layer of all, far beyond the one directly above the troposphere.

options.label: A second, higher troposphere
options.feedback: There is only one troposphere; what sits above it is a distinct layer with its own name and its own behaviour.

options.label: The stratosphere
options.feedback: This layer contains a gas that absorbs sunlight directly, warming the layer as height increases rather than cooling it.

items.ok_line: Straight above the coldest air, the temperature starts climbing again.
items.ko_line: The layer in question sits immediately above the troposphere, not further out.
items.exp_text: In the troposphere, temperature drops the higher you climb, but that trend does not continue forever. Immediately above it sits a layer containing a gas that absorbs incoming sunlight directly, so instead of cooling with height, this layer grows warmer. The layer directly above the troposphere, where temperature starts rising again, is the stratosphere.

items.prompt: Which layer of the whole atmosphere is the coldest?

options.label: The troposphere
options.feedback: The troposphere does cool with height, but it never reaches the coldest point in the whole atmosphere.

options.label: The stratosphere
options.feedback: The stratosphere is warmed by a gas that absorbs sunlight directly, so it does not reach the coldest temperatures.

options.label: The mesosphere
options.feedback: Sitting between two layers that are each warmed from a different direction, this one is warmed by neither.

options.label: The thermosphere
options.feedback: Despite its name, the thermosphere's few scattered molecules move at very high speed, which is not the same as being cold.

items.ok_line: Caught between two layers that each get their own source of heat, this one gets nothing.
items.ko_line: The coldest layer is warmed neither from below nor from above.
items.exp_title: Caught between two sources of warmth
items.exp_text: The troposphere is warmed from below by the ground, and the stratosphere above it is warmed from within by a gas that absorbs sunlight. Sitting between those two warmed layers is one that receives almost none of either kind of warmth. The coldest layer of the whole atmosphere is the mesosphere.

items.prompt: The thermosphere is thin and wispy, yet its temperature can read extremely high. Why?

options.label: Because it lies closest to the sun of all the layers
options.feedback: Every layer of the atmosphere is a negligible distance from the sun compared with how far away the sun actually is; proximity to the sun is not what makes this layer read hot.

options.label: Because a thick blanket of gas traps heat there
options.feedback: The thermosphere is one of the thinnest, least crowded layers of all, the opposite of a thick blanket.

options.label: Because it is packed with the same gases as the ground, only compressed
options.feedback: The gases in the thermosphere are extremely spread out, not compressed; there are very few molecules in a given space.

options.label: Because its few molecules absorb intense solar energy and move at enormous speed
options.feedback: Temperature measures how fast particles move, and here each of the sparse molecules absorbs enough energy to move extremely fast.

items.ok_line: A few molecules moving very fast can register as extreme heat.
items.ko_line: This layer is one of the emptiest of all; the answer has to do with speed, not crowding.
items.exp_title: Heat measured by speed, not by warmth you'd feel
items.exp_text: Temperature is a measure of how fast the particles of a substance are moving, not of how much warmth a body would actually absorb from touching it. In the thermosphere, the handful of molecules present are so spread apart that they rarely collide, and each one absorbs intense solar energy and moves at enormous speed. Its extreme temperature comes from its few molecules absorbing intense solar energy and moving at enormous speed.

items.prompt: What is the name of the outermost layer, where the atmosphere finally fades into space?

options.label: The exosphere
options.feedback: This is the last and thinnest layer, gradually thinning until it merges with the emptiness beyond.

options.label: The stratosphere
options.feedback: The stratosphere lies much closer to the ground, nowhere near where the atmosphere fades into space.

options.label: The mesosphere
options.feedback: The mesosphere is a middle layer, with two further layers still above it before the atmosphere truly fades away.

options.label: The troposphere
options.feedback: The troposphere is the layer closest to the ground, the very opposite end of the atmosphere from where it fades into space.

items.ok_line: Past this one, there's nothing left to call atmosphere at all.
items.ko_line: The outermost layer is the very last stop before open space.
items.exp_text: The atmosphere does not simply stop; it becomes steadily more sparse until only a scattering of particles remains. That final, thinnest stretch is the outermost layer of the whole atmosphere. The outermost layer, where the atmosphere finally fades into space, is the exosphere.

items.prompt: Why does the exosphere have no firm outer edge separating it from space?

options.label: Because it is made of a gas that never runs out
options.feedback: Every gas in the atmosphere becomes sparser with height, including in this outermost layer; nothing about it is inexhaustible.

options.label: Because gravity stops working at that height
options.feedback: Gravity still pulls on particles at that height; it simply grows weaker with distance rather than switching off.

options.label: Because its particles are so far apart that they can drift off into space without colliding with anything
options.feedback: With almost nothing nearby to bump into, a particle moving fast enough in the right direction can simply leave and never come back.

options.label: Because sunlight dissolves the boundary every day
options.feedback: Sunlight warms particles in this layer but does not dissolve or remove any physical boundary.

items.ok_line: Where there's nothing left to collide with, there's nothing left to mark an edge.
items.ko_line: The reason has to do with how spread out the particles are, not with gravity switching off or the gas running low.
items.exp_title: Too spread out to have an edge
items.exp_text: Lower down, air molecules constantly collide with one another, which is part of what makes a layer behave as a connected body of gas. In the exosphere the particles are so far apart that they rarely meet another particle at all. The exosphere has no firm outer edge because its particles are so far apart that they can drift off into space without colliding with anything.

items.prompt: Going up from the ground, in which order do the main layers of the atmosphere sit?

options.label: Mesosphere, troposphere, stratosphere, thermosphere
options.feedback: The mesosphere is a middle layer; it does not come first, right above the ground.

options.label: Troposphere, stratosphere, mesosphere, thermosphere
options.feedback: Starting from the ground, each layer in this order sits further out and behaves differently from the one below it.

options.label: Stratosphere, troposphere, thermosphere, mesosphere
options.feedback: The stratosphere sits above the troposphere, not below it; this order has the first two layers reversed.

options.label: Troposphere, thermosphere, stratosphere, mesosphere
options.feedback: The thermosphere is one of the outermost layers; it does not come second, right after the troposphere.

items.ok_line: Four layers, each one further from the ground than the last.
items.ko_line: Each of these layers has a fixed place in the stack, from the ground outward.
items.exp_text: Closest to the ground sits the layer that holds the air we breathe and the weather we feel. Moving outward from there, each successive layer is warmed or cooled by a different cause than the one below it. Going up from the ground, the main layers sit in the order troposphere, stratosphere, mesosphere, thermosphere.

items.prompt: Why does nearly all the moisture and cloud in the sky stay confined to the lowest layer of the atmosphere?

options.label: Because higher layers are too cold and too dry to hold water in that form
options.feedback: The warmth and water vapour that clouds need are concentrated near the ground, and the layers above are far too cold and thin to sustain them.

options.label: Because clouds are too heavy to rise any further
options.feedback: Clouds are made of tiny droplets carried by rising air currents; weight is not what keeps them confined to one layer.

options.label: Because the higher layers have no gas at all
options.feedback: Every layer of the atmosphere still contains gas, just increasingly thin gas; the higher layers are not truly empty.

options.label: Because sunlight destroys water vapour above a certain height
options.feedback: Sunlight does not destroy water vapour; the reason has to do with warmth and moisture, not sunlight breaking anything apart.

items.ok_title: Kept low by cold and dryness
items.ok_line: The ingredients for cloud are only ever found close to the ground.
items.ko_line: Think about what a cloud actually needs, and where those ingredients are concentrated.
items.exp_title: Where the ingredients for cloud exist
items.exp_text: Clouds form from water vapour that has risen off warm ground and open water, and both that warmth and that moisture are concentrated in the lowest layer. Further up, the air becomes too cold and too thin to carry enough water vapour to form cloud. Nearly all the moisture and cloud in the sky stay confined to the lowest layer because higher layers are too cold and too dry to hold water in that form.
